assessment.summary: The mechanism here is unusually well understood, which is why the probability is rated high rather than speculative: measles needs about 95 percent two-dose coverage to stop circulating, the world is at 77 percent, and the gap translates into outbreaks with an arithmetic reliability that few other threats on this list offer. What makes it a standing threat rather than a solved problem is that the deficit is not primarily technical — the vaccine is cheap, effective and decades old — but a compound of conflict, disrupted health systems and vaccine hesitancy, each of which erodes coverage faster than campaigns rebuild it. The Americas are the clearest warning, having lost and then regained elimination once already before losing it again in November 2025. Severity is continental: measles and its peers kill tens of thousands a year and can paralyse health systems regionally, but they do not threaten civilizational continuity, and the damage is reversible by the same tool that caused the decline when it went unused.
assessment.timeframe: Under way now: coverage has hovered in the same narrow range since 2009, and elimination status has been withdrawn from four countries in the Americas within twelve months.

claims.text: WHO's measles fact sheet (last updated 15 July 2026) states that "An estimated 95 000 people died from measles in 2024" and that "Measles vaccination averted nearly 59 million deaths between 2000 and 2024."

The WHO/UNICEF immunization coverage estimates released 15 July 2026 report 2025 measles coverage "with 84% of children receiving the first measles dose (MCV1) and 77% receiving the second dose (MCV2)", adding that "Both figures fall far short of the 95% threshold required to prevent outbreaks of this highly contagious virus" and that "57 countries reported large or disruptive measles outbreaks in 2025."

The same WHO/UNICEF release states that "an estimated 13.5 million 'zero-dose' children did not receive a single vaccine in their first year during 2025", and that global coverage has been "hovering within the same narrow range since 2009".

PAHO announced on 10 November 2025 that "the Region of the Americas has lost its verification as free from endemic measles transmission" after endemic transmission was re-established in Canada, where the virus had circulated for at least 12 months. As of 7 November 2025 the region had recorded 12 596 confirmed cases across ten countries - about 30 times the 2024 count - and 28 deaths, with second-dose MMR coverage averaging 79 percent in 2024, well below the 95 percent needed to prevent outbreaks.

PAHO's technical reference of 17 November 2026 states that following the sixth annual meeting of the Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission (10-13 November 2026), the United States, Mexico and Bolivia were also found to have lost national measles elimination status, the virus having "circulated continuously in each country for at least 12 months". As of epidemiological week 44 (6 November 2026) "58,213 measles cases have been reported by member countries and territories", with 114 deaths, and regional routine coverage in 2025 "reached only 88% for the first dose of measles vaccine and 85% for the second dose".

PAHO, reporting WHO estimates on 28 November 2025, states that measles caused "an estimated 11 million infections in 2024" and that "an estimated 95 000 people, mostly children younger than 5 years of age, died due to measles in 2024", a fall of 88 percent in deaths between 2000 and 2024, with 59 countries reporting large or disruptive measles outbreaks in 2024.

description: Diseases that vaccination had pushed to the margins are returning, because immunisation coverage has stalled well below the level needed to stop them spreading. Measles is the indicator, since it is the most contagious of them and the first to come back when coverage slips: WHO estimates 95 000 deaths and around 11 million infections in 2024, and global coverage in 2025 stood at 84 percent for the first measles dose and 77 percent for the second, far short of the 95 percent needed to prevent outbreaks. An estimated 13.5 million children received no vaccine at all in their first year of life in 2025, and 57 countries reported large or disruptive measles outbreaks. The loss of hard-won ground is already formal: the Americas lost their region-wide measles elimination verification in November 2025, and in November 2026 the regional commission found endemic transmission re-established in the United States, Mexico and Bolivia as well. Vaccination still averted nearly 59 million deaths between 2000 and 2024, which is what is being eroded.
name: Resurgence of Vaccine-Preventable Disease
